ch2.a1.steps:
Split into four groups.
1. Group A: 50 mL of water and one spatula of copper sulphate.
2. Group B: 50 mL of water and two spatulas of copper sulphate.
3. Groups C and D: mix different amounts of copper sulphate with potassium permanganate, or salt with sulphur.
4. Compare colour and texture across all four.
ch2.a1.watchFor: A and B are both uniform and yet clearly different in colour. C and D are not uniform at all. What separates the two behaviours?
ch2.a2.steps:
1. Group A: a few copper sulphate crystals in water. Group B: a spatula of copper sulphate. Group C: chalk powder or wheat flour. Group D: a few drops of milk or ink.
2. Stir each one properly with a glass rod. Can you see the particles?
3. Shine a torch beam through each beaker from the side and look from the front. Can you see the beam's path?
4. Leave them all standing for a few minutes. Does anything settle?
5. Filter each one. Is there anything on the filter paper?
ch2.a2.watchFor: Fill in a table as you go: visible particles, torch beam visible, settles, leaves a residue. Three different patterns will appear.
ch2.a3.steps:
1. Put about 50 mL of water in each of two beakers.
2. Add salt to one and sugar or barium chloride to the other, stirring all the time.
3. Stop when no more will dissolve. Write down how much went in.
4. Heat both beakers to raise the temperature by about 5 degrees.
5. Start adding again.
ch2.a3.watchFor: Does the same amount of salt and sugar dissolve? Does warming let you add more? Now let one cool slowly and watch what appears.
ch2.a4.steps:
Your teacher must supervise this one.
Split into two groups. Both get 5 g of iron filings and 3 g of sulphur powder in a china dish.
1. Group I: mix and crush them together. Stop there.
2. Group II: mix, crush, then heat strongly until red hot. Remove from the flame and let it cool.
3. Both groups: hold a magnet near the material.
4. Both groups: add carbon disulphide to one part, stir and filter.
5. Both groups: add dilute acid to the other part and smell the gas carefully.
ch2.a4.watchFor: You started with the same two things. Compare colour, texture, magnetism, and above all the smell of the gas. Group I gets odourless hydrogen. Group II gets hydrogen sulphide, which smells of rotten eggs.
ch2.drivingQuestion: Is anything around you actually just one thing?
ch2.groupActivity.steps:
1. Take an earthen pot, or matka, with a small hole in the base.
2. Lay a piece of cloth at the bottom.
3. Add a layer of fine sand, then coarse sand, then pebbles on top.
4. Pour muddy water in slowly at the top and collect what comes out.
ch2.groupActivity.watchFor: Compare what went in with what came out. Then ask yourself what the filter could not possibly have removed.
ch2.item.air.why: A solution of gases in a gas, mostly nitrogen with oxygen dissolved in it. A solution does not have to be a liquid.
ch2.item.boilingWater.why: Physical, even though it looks violent. Steam is still water, and it condenses straight back.
ch2.item.brass.why: A solid solution of about 30 percent zinc in 70 percent copper. Alloys are solutions too.
ch2.item.burningPaper.why: Chemical. Ash, smoke and gases, none of which is paper, and no way back.
ch2.item.chalkWater.why: Settles when left alone and is removed completely by a filter.
ch2.item.creamFromMilk.why: Milk is a colloid, so a filter is useless. Spinning it hard forces the lighter fat to separate.
ch2.item.cuttingTrees.why: The wood is still wood. Only its size and shape changed.
ch2.item.digestion.why: Chemical. Your body breaks food into entirely different substances it can absorb.
ch2.item.dissolvingSalt.why: Physical, even though the salt vanishes. Boil the water off and the salt is back, unchanged.
ch2.item.electrolysis: Passing electricity through water until it splits into hydrogen and oxygen
ch2.item.electrolysis.why: Chemical. Two new substances appeared, and neither of them is water.
ch2.item.fog.why: Water droplets dispersed in air. It scatters light, which is exactly why you cannot see through it.
ch2.item.freezingWater.why: Physical. Same substance, different arrangement, fully reversible.
ch2.item.fruitSalad.why: Every piece of fruit is still itself. Cutting and mixing changes nothing chemically.
ch2.item.meltingButter.why: Still butter, just liquid. Cool it and it comes back.
ch2.item.milk.why: Fat droplets too small to see or filter, but big enough to scatter light. The classic colloid.
ch2.item.muddyWater.why: Visible particles that settle out and catch on filter paper.
ch2.item.plantGrowth.why: Chemical. The plant builds sugars and tissue out of carbon dioxide, water and minerals.
ch2.item.rustingAlmirah.why: Chemical. Iron plus oxygen and water makes iron oxide, a new substance you cannot turn back into iron by cooling it.
ch2.item.saltFromSeaWater: Getting salt out of sea water
ch2.item.saltFromSeaWater.why: Let the water evaporate and the dissolved salt is left behind. This is how coastal salt pans work.
ch2.item.saltSolution.why: Particles below a nanometre. No scattering, no settling, nothing on the filter paper.
ch2.item.shavingCream.why: Gas dispersed through a liquid, which makes it a foam, one of the colloid types.
ch2.item.sodaWater.why: Carbon dioxide gas dissolved in water. A gas in a liquid is still a solution.
ch2.item.starchSolution.why: Called a solution in everyday speech, but starch particles are large enough to scatter light. It is a colloid.
ch2.item.teaLeaves: Getting tea leaves out of tea
ch2.item.teaLeaves.why: The leaves are an undissolved suspension, so a strainer catches them.
ch2.item.waterFromInk: Getting pure water back out of ink
ch2.item.waterFromInk.why: Boil the water off and condense the vapour somewhere else. The dye stays behind.
ch2.title: Is Matter Around Us Pure?
ch2.u1.check.a: No. It is unadulterated, but it is still a mixture of sugars, water and other compounds
ch2.u1.check.a.fb: Right. Honest labelling and scientific purity are two different claims. Honey is unadulterated and it is a mixture.
ch2.u1.check.b: Yes, because nothing has been added to it
ch2.u1.check.b.fb: That is the shopkeeper's definition, not the chemist's. Adding nothing does not make something one kind of particle. Honey was a mixture before anyone bottled it.
ch2.u1.check.c: Yes, because it comes from a single natural source
ch2.u1.check.c.fb: Coming from one place says nothing about what is in it. Sea water comes from one source and contains dozens of substances. Purity is about the particles, not the origin.
ch2.u1.check.prompt: A bottle is labelled pure honey and the contents are exactly what the label says. Is it a pure substance?
ch2.u1.definition: A pure substance is made of one kind of particle, all the way through, whatever its source. Salt from the sea and salt from a mine are the same substance with the same properties. That is what makes purity worth defining.
ch2.u1.goal: Replace the everyday meaning of pure with the scientific one, by making the everyday meaning fail.
ch2.u1.labels.caption: Sort them once the way a shopper would. Then sort them again the way a chemist would, and watch your own answers move.
ch2.u1.observe.explanation: Neither. They are using the same word for two different things. On a packet, pure means nothing has been added that should not be there. In science, pure means every particle in it is the same kind. Milk is honest about what is in it and it is still water, fat, protein and sugar together, so it is a mixture. Only distilled water and the copper wire pass the scientific test.
ch2.u1.observe.prompt: Every one of those packets says pure, and a chemist would call almost all of them mixtures. Who is wrong?
ch2.u1.title: What the word pure actually means
ch2.u2.check.a.fb: Correct. Both are colloids, so their particles are the right size to scatter a light beam. The two true solutions let the light straight through.
ch2.u2.check.b: Only milk, because starch eventually settles at the bottom
ch2.u2.check.b.fb: Starch does not settle. Colloid particles are too small to be pulled down, which is why a colloid is described as stable. Leave it overnight and it is still cloudy.
ch2.u2.check.c: All four, because filter paper would catch something from each
ch2.u2.check.c.fb: Filtering does not work on solutions or colloids. Only a suspension leaves a residue. Colloids need centrifugation, and a solution cannot be separated by either.
ch2.u2.check.prompt: Which of these would show the Tyndall effect: salt solution, milk, copper sulphate solution, starch solution?
ch2.u2.goal: Classify a mixture from evidence you gathered, not from a definition you memorised, and connect the three classes to particle size.
ch2.u2.mixturemaker.caption: Add different amounts and look for uniformity. Some of these stay even throughout and some refuse to.
ch2.u2.observe.explanation: Particle size explains all three patterns at once. In a solution the particles are smaller than a nanometre, too small to scatter light and too small for any filter, and they never settle. In a suspension they are big enough to see, to catch on filter paper and to sink. A colloid sits in between: too small to see or to filter or to settle, but big enough to scatter a light beam. That scattering is called the Tyndall effect.
ch2.u2.observe.prompt: The milk never settled and never passed through the filter, and yet the torch beam showed up in it. What does that combination mean?
ch2.u2.predict.prompt: You leave all three standing overnight. Which ones will have settled by morning?
ch2.u2.predict0.depends: Group B will be patchy because there is more powder
ch2.u2.predict0.patchy: Both patchy, with darker regions at the bottom
ch2.u2.predict0.prompt: Groups A and B both dissolved copper sulphate, but different amounts. What will their mixtures look like?
ch2.u2.sort.prompt: Sort these by what they would do under the torch, the filter and a night standing still.
ch2.u2.threeBeakers.caption: Run every test on every sample and fill the table. Only name them once the table is complete.
ch2.u2.title: Solution, suspension, colloid
ch2.u2.tyndall: You have seen the Tyndall effect many times. Sunlight through the canopy of a forest, where mist droplets hang in the air. A beam through a gap in a door, lit up by dust. Headlights in fog. In every case something too small to see is scattering the light and making the beam visible.
ch2.u2.zoom.caption: Three new stops on the scale. The line at one nanometre is the boundary between a solution and everything else.
ch2.u3.calc1.given1: Mass of solute, the salt, is 40 g
ch2.u3.calc1.given2: Mass of solvent, the water, is 320 g
ch2.u3.calc1.prompt: A solution contains 40 g of common salt in 320 g of water. Find the concentration as a mass by mass percentage.
ch2.u3.calc1.step1: Mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent = 40 + 320 = 360 g
ch2.u3.calc1.step2: Percentage = (mass of solute divided by mass of solution) times 100 = (40 / 360) times 100
ch2.u3.calc1.trap: Dividing by 320 instead of 360. The denominator is the mass of the whole solution, which includes the salt you added. This single error loses more marks than anything else in the chapter.
ch2.u3.calc2.prompt: To make a saturated solution, 36 g of sodium chloride is dissolved in 100 g of water at 293 K. Find the concentration.
ch2.u3.calc2.trap: Answering 36 percent by dividing by the 100 g of water. Again, the denominator is the whole solution.
ch2.u3.calc3.given1: Solubility of potassium nitrate at 313 K is 62 g per 100 g of water
ch2.u3.calc3.prompt: From the solubility table, potassium nitrate has a solubility of 62 g per 100 g of water at 313 K. What mass would saturate 50 g of water at that temperature?
ch2.u3.calc3.step1: Half the water holds half the solute, so 62 divided by 2
ch2.u3.calc3.trap: Using 62 g directly without halving it. Solubility is always quoted per 100 g of water, so read the water mass in the question before you answer.
ch2.u3.check.a: Crystals appearing, because cooler water holds less than hot water could
ch2.u3.check.a.fb: Right. Solubility falls as the temperature drops, so the water cannot hold all of it any more and the excess crystallises out. This is how sugar candy is made.
ch2.u3.check.b: Nothing, because the dissolved salt has been destroyed and cannot come back
ch2.u3.check.b.fb: Dissolving never destroys anything. The salt was there the whole time, spread through the water, and cooling brings it back as visible crystals. That is the proof.
ch2.u3.check.c: The solution will freeze solid, because dissolving is a kind of melting
ch2.u3.check.c.fb: Dissolving and melting are different. Melting needs heat to break a solid apart on its own. Dissolving spreads a solid through a liquid at ordinary temperature. Room temperature is nowhere near freezing either.
ch2.u3.check.prompt: Pragya makes a saturated potassium chloride solution at 353 K and leaves it to cool to room temperature. What will she see?
ch2.u3.goal: Define saturation and solubility from an experiment, and calculate concentration without falling into the mass-of-solution trap.
ch2.u3.observe.explanation: The amount that dissolves at a given temperature is the solubility, and it is different for every substance. Potassium nitrate climbs steeply with temperature, while sodium chloride is almost flat. This is why cooling a hot saturated solution makes crystals appear: the liquid can no longer hold what it was holding, so the excess comes back out as solid.
ch2.u3.observe.prompt: Look at your four curves. Which substance changes the most with temperature, and which barely changes at all?
ch2.u3.predict.lessDissolves: Some of the dissolved salt comes back out
ch2.u3.predict.noChange: Nothing changes, it is already full
ch2.u3.predict.prompt: No more salt will dissolve. You warm the beaker by 20 degrees. What happens?
ch2.u3.solubility.caption: Spoon it in until it stops going. Then move the temperature. The curve plots itself as you work.
ch2.u3.title: How much will dissolve
ch2.u4.candle.caption: Watch the wax near the flame and the wax in the flame. They are not doing the same thing.
ch2.u4.check.a: Dissolving salt is physical, rusting iron is chemical
ch2.u4.check.a.fb: Right. Salt comes back when you boil the water off. Rust does not come back as iron no matter what you do to it.
ch2.u4.check.b: Dissolving salt is chemical because the salt disappears, boiling water is chemical because it is violent
ch2.u4.check.b.fb: Neither is chemical. How dramatic a change looks tells you nothing. Boiling looks violent and makes no new substance. Rusting looks like nothing at all and does.
ch2.u4.check.c: Dissolving is a kind of melting, so both are physical for the same reason
ch2.u4.check.c.fb: Both are physical, but not for the same reason. Melting is a solid becoming liquid on its own with heat. Dissolving is a solid spreading through a different liquid. Salt dissolves in cold water and does not melt until about 1074 K.
ch2.u4.check.prompt: Which of these pairs is correctly labelled?
ch2.u4.goal: Separate physical from chemical change using one test, whether a new substance appeared.
ch2.u4.intro: There is only one question worth asking: is there a new substance at the end that was not there at the start? If yes, it is a chemical change. If no, it is physical, however dramatic it looked. Ice, water and steam look completely different and are chemically the same thing, so all the changes between them are physical.
ch2.u4.observe.explanation: The wax near the flame melts and runs down the side, and that is physical, because it is still wax and it sets again. The wax drawn up the wick burns, and that is chemical, because it becomes carbon dioxide and water vapour and is gone for good. One object, both kinds of change, which is why a candle is the standard example.
ch2.u4.observe.prompt: Two different things are happening to the same wax at the same time. What are they?
ch2.u4.predict.prompt: A candle is burning. Is that a physical change or a chemical one?
ch2.u4.sort.prompt: Physical or chemical? Ask only one question: is there a new substance at the end?
ch2.u4.title: Did you make something new?
ch2.u5.check.a: Like salt, because a compound has its own properties that have nothing to do with its elements
ch2.u5.check.a.fb: Exactly. This is the single most important idea in the chapter. Combining chemically produces something genuinely new, not a blend of what went in.
ch2.u5.check.b: Dangerous, because it still contains a violent metal and a poisonous gas mixed together
ch2.u5.check.b.fb: They are not mixed together, they are chemically combined, and that is the whole difference. A mixture of sodium and chlorine would indeed be dangerous. The compound is on your dinner.
ch2.u5.check.c: It would be a liquid, since one of its elements is a gas
ch2.u5.check.c.fb: A compound's state is its own. Sodium is a solid, chlorine a gas, and sodium chloride is a solid crystal that melts at over 1000 K. You cannot predict a compound's properties from its elements.
ch2.u5.check.prompt: Sodium is a soft metal that reacts violently with water. Chlorine is a poisonous green gas. What does sodium chloride taste like on your food?
ch2.u5.classifyForward.caption: Drop each substance in at the top and answer the questions on the way down.
ch2.u5.classifyReverse.caption: Now the other way round. You are given a position on the tree. Name something that belongs there.
ch2.u5.goal: Show that a compound has properties of its own, unrelated to the elements that made it, while a mixture keeps the properties of its parts.
ch2.u5.ironSulphur.caption: Same starting materials, two paths. Run all four tests on both and let the table build itself.
ch2.u5.mixtureVsCompound: A mixture can be made in any proportion, shows the properties of its parts, and comes apart by physical means. A compound has a fixed composition, has properties of its own that its elements do not, and comes apart only by a chemical reaction. Group I made a mixture. Group II made a compound.
ch2.u5.observe.explanation: Nowhere. Every iron particle is still in the dish. But it is no longer iron. Heating made the iron and sulphur combine into iron sulphide, a single new substance with its own properties, and those properties have nothing to do with iron or sulphur. It is not magnetic, carbon disulphide will not pull the sulphur back out, and acid gives a completely different gas. The unheated mixture kept both sets of properties because it was still two substances sitting next to each other.
ch2.u5.observe.prompt: The heated sample ignored the magnet completely. Where did the iron go?
ch2.u5.predict.bothMagnetic: Both, the iron is still in there either way
ch2.u5.predict.heatedOnly: Only the group that heated it
ch2.u5.predict.mixedOnly: Only the group that just mixed
ch2.u5.predict.prompt: Both groups started with iron filings. Which one will still be attracted to a magnet at the end?
ch2.u5.predict0.prompt: Which single test best separates metals from non-metals?
ch2.u5.propertyTester.caption: Five tests, eight samples. Run them and see which test is the reliable one.
ch2.u5.title: Elements, compounds, and the difference a mixture cannot fake
ch2.u6.challenge.brief: You have an earthen pot, pebbles, coarse sand, fine sand, charcoal and a piece of cloth. Layer them to build a small filtration plant and get muddy water as clear as you can.
ch2.u6.challenge.debrief: Coarse at the top and fine at the bottom works best, because each layer catches what the one above it let through. This is how a village sand filter and a municipal water works both operate, at completely different scales and on the same principle.
ch2.u6.check.a: Check that it boils at exactly 373 K and freezes at exactly 273 K at normal pressure
ch2.u6.check.a.fb: Right. A pure substance has a sharp, fixed melting and boiling point. Anything dissolved in the water shifts those points, so the thermometer gives it away.
ch2.u6.check.b: Look at it. If it is completely clear and colourless, it is pure
ch2.u6.check.b.fb: You just saw filtered muddy water pass that test and fail the torch test. Sea water is clear too. Your eyes cannot detect anything dissolved.
ch2.u6.check.c: Filter it. If nothing is left on the paper, it is pure
ch2.u6.check.c.fb: Filtering cannot remove dissolved substances or colloids. A salt solution passes straight through filter paper leaving nothing behind, and it is certainly not pure water.
ch2.u6.check.prompt: You are handed a colourless liquid and told it is pure water. How would you check?
ch2.u6.clearCheck.caption: One test. Shine the torch through your clear filtered water.
ch2.u6.goal: Build a working filter, then discover that clear is not the same as pure.
ch2.u6.observe.explanation: Filtering only removes suspension-sized particles. Anything colloidal is still in the water, scattering your torch beam, and anything dissolved is still there too and would not scatter light at all. Clear water can hold dissolved salts, minerals and microbes. Clear is a statement about what you can see. Pure is a statement about what is actually in it.
ch2.u6.observe.prompt: It looks clear and the torch beam still shows up. What is left in there?
ch2.u6.predict.prompt: Your filtered water is completely clear. Is it pure?
ch2.u6.predict.stillMixture: No, it is still a mixture
ch2.u6.predict.yesPure: Yes, there is nothing visible left in it

ch2.u7.goal: Meet the standard separation techniques, which this edition of the textbook leaves out.
ch2.u7.notice: This unit is extra. The 2026-27 Karnataka textbook removed the separation techniques section from Chapter 2, so none of this will be examined from that chapter. It is here because the summary page still mentions separation, because other boards still teach it, and because it is genuinely useful. Treat it as optional.
ch2.u7.sort.prompt: Which technique would you use for each job?
ch2.u7.title: Bonus: separating mixtures
mis.colloidsSettle.correction: They will not. Colloid particles are too small to be pulled down, which is why a colloid is called stable.
mis.colloidsSettle.statement: Colloid particles will settle if you wait long enough.
mis.compoundIsWellMixedMixture.correctio: A compound has fixed composition and properties of its own. Sodium and chlorine are dangerous, and sodium chloride is table salt.
mis.compoundIsWellMixedMixture.statement: A compound is just a thoroughly mixed mixture.
mis.dissolvingDestroys.correction: It is only spread out. Boil the water away and the solid comes back unchanged.
mis.dissolvingDestroys.statement: When something dissolves it is destroyed or turns into the liquid.
mis.dissolvingIsMelting.correction: Melting is a solid becoming liquid by itself with heat. Dissolving is a solid spreading through another liquid, often in the cold.
mis.dissolvingIsMelting.statement: Dissolving and melting are the same process.
mis.dramaticMeansChemical.correction: Boiling looks violent and makes nothing new. Rusting looks like nothing and makes a new substance. Only the new-substance test counts.
mis.dramaticMeansChemical.statement: A violent or dramatic change must be chemical.
mis.filteringSeparatesAnything.correctio: Only a suspension leaves a residue. Colloids need centrifuging and solutions cannot be filtered at all.
mis.pureMeansClean.correction: In science it means one kind of particle. Honest, unadulterated milk is still a mixture.
mis.pureMeansClean.statement: Pure means clean, healthy or unadulterated.
mis.solutionMustBeLiquid.correction: Air is a solution of gases and brass is a solution of solids. What matters is uniformity at particle level, not state.
mis.solutionMustBeLiquid.statement: A solution has to be a liquid.
